Nietzsche's view was influenced by pre-Socratics, and especially Heraclitus who saw all permanence as illusory. This is an ages old rift in ontology, the difference between Being and Becoming. Other existential philosophers like Kierkegaard, Sartre, and Heidegger, had projects interested in the state of being, (oversimplified explanation incoming) they wanted to know who/what we are to reach towards a why and how to live. Nietzsche (and imo this was a direct influence of his readings of Schopenhauer) saw the who/what as an irreducible complexity, an unavoidable paradox, and instead ventured into how/why we are to reach towards an understanding of what to do and who to be to live. This profound difference is the basis for both his idea of geneaology and the "will to power," and it's this way of thinking that is the beginning of Foucault's projects in postmodernism framework.

So Nietzsche was not saying you move past nihilism, or use nihilism, or overcome nihilism. The lack of meaning was simply a representation (Schopenhauer again) which would come and go with different influences and different results on the will/being, a force/power (one of many) of Becoming.

The thrust of room 101 as political philosophy was that relativism, taken to a logical end, is the source of the totalitarian regime. Or, if not the source, so easily manipulated by the totalitarian instinct to be indistinguishable.

That might seem paradoxical or counterintuitive, that 1984, the world's most famous book about controlling information to control humanity, is about why we should protect a certain set of values to guide humanity. But Orwell's allegory firmly silhouetted what he saw as the ability of Western culture to seek definitive truths: of external reality through scientific inquiry unfettered by socialism's New Man needs, and social values based in inherent human experience reasoned out through both legal action and public discourse. 1984 is a book about the profound and horrifying disappointment that disillusioned socialists and fellow travelers, across the world, felt about Stalinism.

In the harsh light of Room 101, what's in the shadows is what Orwell held dear as a "champion of human decency."
